title: NASA FLEX (PSI-69) — n-Heptane Droplet d² Combustion & Cool Flame

measurementSeries.note: Hot flame radiative extinction (flame vanishes optically)
Invisible quasi-steady cool flame burning at ~650 K

calibration.algorithm: Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) regression over quasi-steady hot flame period [0.5, 6.5 s]
limits: Valid strictly for isolated n-heptane droplets in quiescent air (18-21% O2, 101.3 kPa, 0g).
Does not capture the post-extinction cool flame regime (t > 6.8s) where burning rate drops to K ≈ 0.31 mm²/s.
Must not be applied to other fuels, solid polymers, or convective airflow environments.
calibration.notes: Fitted K=0.76 mm²/s accurately matches the hot flame burn period. The cool-flame transition at t=6.8s demonstrates the physical failure boundary of single-stage d² theory.

userControls.label: Initial Droplet Diameter (D₀)
userControls.validDomain: 1.5 to 4.5 mm (NASA FLEX flight sample sizes)
userControls.effectDescription: Governs initial surface area (D₀²), soot shell retention, and total burn lifetime.

userControls.label: Burning Rate Constant (K)
userControls.effectDescription: Slope of droplet surface area regression d(D²)/dt during hot flame phase.

userControls.label: Ambient Oxygen Concentration
userControls.effectDescription: Observed test condition. Changing O2 requires multi-run empirical calibration curve; locked in calibrated mode.

userControls.label: Gravitational Acceleration
userControls.effectDescription: Locked at 0g. Scientific rule: microgravity results cannot be quantitatively scaled to 1g, Lunar (0.16g), or Martian (0.38g) gravity without empirical partial-gravity test records.

citation.sourceLocator: PSI Investigation Record PSI-69 / Nayagam et al., Combustion and Flame 159 (2012)
citation.title: Can cool flames support quasi-steady alkane droplet burning?
citation.authors: V. Nayagam, D. L. Dietrich, P. V. Ferkul, M. C. Hicks, F. A. Williams

allowed: The calibrated d² law with K = 0.76 mm²/s models the linear hot flame regression (t = 0.5 to 6.5s) with high fidelity (RMSE = 0.038 mm²).
NASA FLEX measurements show that the droplet does not burn to completion under hot flame: radiative extinction occurs at D ≈ 1.87 mm.
Post-extinction cool flame burning continues at a significantly reduced rate (K ≈ 0.31 mm²/s) without visible emission, presenting an invisible spacecraft fire hazard.
disallowed: Do not extrapolate the K=0.76 value to higher airflow or elevated oxygen without separate calibration datasets.
Do not use this single-droplet model to predict bulk polymer or cabin material flammability.
Do not claim quantitative predictive accuracy for Lunar (0.16g) or Martian (0.38g) partial gravity environments.

citation.sourceLocator: PSI Investigation Record PSI-98 / Urban et al., Combustion and Flame 2019
citation.title: Flame spread: Effects of microgravity and scale
citation.authors: D. L. Urban, P. Ferkul, S. Olson, G. A. Ruff, J. T. Easton

sourceMedia.caption: Cygnus flight flow duct geometry (0.4m x 1.0m sample array with radiometers).
sourceMedia.nasaCredit: NASA Glenn Research Center Saffire Team

allowed: Large-scale solid fabric fires in microgravity burn steadily and continuously under standard cabin airflow (20 cm/s).
Absence of buoyant smoke convection means heat transfer is governed strictly by forced airflow and radiative loss.
disallowed: Do not use small NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 upward burning results to certify large vehicle materials.
Do not extrapolate these results to quiescent (< 2 cm/s) environments where fabric flammability extinguishes.

title: NASA BASS-II (PSI-87) — Opposed-Flow Solid PMMA Quenching
investigation: BASS-II Burning and Suppression of Solids (ISS MSG)

measurementSeries.note: Hot wire ignition on PMMA edge
Quasi-steady spread rate at 3.5 cm/s flow
Sustained combustion with radiative soot halo
Radiative extinction boundary reached as flow throttles

userControls.label: Opposed Airflow Velocity
userControls.effectDescription: At low flow (< 2 cm/s), radiative cooling exceeds thermal generation, causing unexpected flame extinction.

citation.sourceLocator: PSI-87 / Bhattacharjee et al., Fire Safety Journal 2016
citation.title: Opposed-flow flame spread: A comparison of microgravity and normal gravity experiments
citation.authors: S. Bhattacharjee, K. Takahashi, M. Wakai

sourceMedia.caption: BASS-II microgravity opposed-flow flame spread and radiative quenching series aboard ISS MSG.

allowed: In low-speed microgravity flow, thick PMMA exhibits non-monotonic spread rates due to radiative quenching.
Extinction in microgravity can occur from thermal cooling rather than fuel starvation.
disallowed: Do not assume quiescent (0 cm/s) conditions are the safest: smoldering can persist without visible flame.

allowed: In microgravity without buoyant updraft, solid flame fronts exhibit periodic pulsations governed by fuel vaporization and diffusion expansion.
Frames verify 0.2-second interval sequence released by NASA SVS.
disallowed: Do not infer quantitative numerical gas concentrations from raw pixel brightness.
